title: Why you shouldn't listen to Genetic Freaks (The Joel Williams Example)
summary: NH critiques Joel Williams' how-to-get-huge-arms video (compounds first, pump chasing, short rests, strapless back work for forearms) and argues for isolation, progressive overload, proper rest and straps. He then explains that genetic freaks give bad advice because everything works for them, ranks genetics on a 1-10 scale, tells the story of a Nigerian roommate who got shredded doing almost nothing, and warns about contrarian influencers using the Mentzer formula.
claims: The claim that 70% of arm gains come from compounds is made up; it is only true if you do nothing but compounds
If you only bench and overhead press, 100% of your triceps gains come from them, which proves nothing about their effectiveness
The idea that isolation gives definition and striations while compounds give size is debunked bro science; striations come from leanness, every resistance exercise grows muscle
Lifting more total weight on compounds does not make them better for hypertrophy of a specific muscle, because the load is spread across several muscles and joints
For maximally challenging the triceps, a pushdown beats the bench press; isolation is strictly superior for growing specific arm muscles
Very few people are triceps-dominant on bench; leverage favors chest and shoulders, so bench strength carries over little to triceps size
Everyone who gets stronger on pushdowns gets bigger triceps; the minority who grow huge triceps from bench alone are outliers
A four-plate chin-up does not guarantee big biceps; chin-ups are primarily a lat movement, and half that strength progression on curls gives better biceps results
No grip tweak turns a pulldown into a biceps exercise unless the shoulder is stationary and only the elbow moves, which is an isolation movement
Shoulders differ from arms: 70-80% of shoulder gains can come from horizontal and vertical presses because front and side delts respond well to them, though you still want raises and rear delt work
Treating arm isolation as mere accessory work leads to imbalance between a big torso and small arms
Compounds are essential and should make up the bulk of a program, but bench counts as triceps volume and fatigue to account for, not as a triceps exercise
Over-focusing on fatiguing compounds leaves no energy for isolation, so arms get no direct volume
Experimenting with high volume on arm isolation and adding an arm day are good advice since isolation volume is easy to recover from
A rookie mistake is using baby weights on isolation; once you progressively overload arm isolation you grow
A rep range is not a magic number but a bracket to get close to failure and progress within; without high intensity you plateau regardless of the range
In terms of intensity and progression arms are like every other muscle; only their biomechanical function needs specific targeting
The pump is at best an accessory; chasing it leads to high reps with light weights and no attention to failure or load
Take 2-3 minutes between arm exercises for the same muscle; supersets of different muscles are fine, performance matters for biceps as much as quads
Stuck curling the same 30s for a year, you won't grow however good the pump; muscle adapts to tension, not to blood
Intensity techniques like drop sets and cluster sets are fine within quality volume with relevant weight and rest, not as empty-bar pump work
Going strapless on back work does not build forearms; most people lift without straps and still have stick forearms
Not using straps tires your grip so you have nothing left for direct forearm training, and gripping is a secondary function giving minimal hypertrophy
Use straps on back work so the weak grip doesn't limit your back, and train forearms directly (e.g. hammer curls); forearm isolation costs only 10-15 minutes a week
Genetic freaks give bad advice not out of stupidity or malice but because everything works for them so they can't tell what works
Joel built an elite physique in about 3 years, better than 99% of naturals; NH believes he is natural
People attribute successes to their own effort and failures to external causes, so gifted influencers credit their hard work rather than genetics
He estimates true 10/10 genetic freaks at about 0.2% of the population
A genetic freak looks incredible without training or explodes in size from random training or almost nothing
His Nigerian grad-school roommate trained 40 min twice a week with a randomizer app, only 4 months a year, no legs, ate junk, yet was 6 ft, 185 lb, 8% bodyfat with a Greek-god physique
He rates genetics: freaks 10, Alex Leonidas around 6-7, Geoffrey Verity Schofield 6-7, himself a 5; a 7 versus a 10 is like an IM versus a GM in chess
Joel achieved in 3 years what NH achieved in 15
Take advice from a 5-7 who had to figure out how to keep growing; a 10 cannot teach, like his genius Korean stats professor or Mikhail Tal playing on instinct
Social media rewards the biggest freaks with visibility, so average fives take advice from tens and get poor results that make them think they lack potential
There is nothing wrong with being average; he is Mr Average and reached a high level in multiple disciplines by hard work and right methods
Don't harass Joel; envying people with better genetics is pathetic, work with what you have
Some influencers give bad advice on purpose (e.g. weighted pull-ups for big biceps) because contrarianism gets attention
Intermediate curl strength reliably grows biceps, while elite pull-up strength may not
Mentzer's method is ineffective but spread because he was a charismatic contrarian who looked like a 10; on social media the promoter's physique matters more than the method
Spot bad influencers by their contrarian everyone-else-is-wrong or edgy I-do-it-differently attitude
Prefer advice from people who look like they lift, but keep critical thinking
People with good genetics get their physique despite subpar methods, not because of them; a method that works only for outliers is useless
He treats the channel as a secondary job funded by Ko-fi pledges
